title: Trump Rules Out Cyberattack as FAA Ground Stop Probe Points to Overloaded Aging Network
excerpt: The nationwide ground stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday after more than four hours. FlightAware counted 5,117 US cancellations on Friday; Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed routers overloaded on a legacy system.
body:
• President Donald Trump said the nationwide flight disruption was unlikely to have been caused by a cyberattack or artificial intelligence, attributing it to aging, broken equipment in the FAA's infrastructure.
  • The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET on Friday, November 13, more than four hours after it was imposed shortly before 4 p.m. ET.
  • FlightAware counted 9,814 delays and 5,117 cancellations within, into or out of the United States on Friday, and an analysis by Cirium estimated 1.5 million travellers were stranded.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said instability began at 3:36 p.m. ET, blamed routers overloaded with data on the legacy telecommunications network, and is asking Congress for up to $50 billion to replace the system.

President Donald Trump has ruled out a cyberattack or artificial intelligence as the cause of Friday's nationwide flight disruption, saying the Federal Aviation Administration's failure came from old equipment rather than an adversary.

Trump gave his account in a phone call relayed by Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy: it does not look like a cyberattack or AI-related, he said, and nobody has claimed credit — which, he noted, is common after a large attack on critical infrastructure, making the silence itself evidence. His alternative explanation was "a bunch of old broken stuff in the infrastructure that the FAA relies on to keep planes in the sky," including equipment he described as 55 years old. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin gave the same assessment from the White House: "We have seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack. It appears this was mechanically driven."

What failed, on the official account

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy put the start of the failure at 3:36 p.m. ET on Friday, when the FAA saw instability in radar and communications systems at air traffic control centres and TRACON facilities nationwide. More than 3,500 aircraft were airborne when the ground stop was ordered. Duffy blamed an overloaded legacy analog telecommunications network: routers "overloaded with data," producing inconsistency in the information they supplied, according to Implicator's summary of the briefings.

The FAA's own advisory, issued shortly before 4 p.m. ET, ordered the national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety," citing communication issues affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers, People reported. The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure network at the centre of the failure is operated by L3Harris. A separate account pointed to a network or software update at the operator; no official has confirmed what triggered the overload, and L3Harris had not responded to requests for comment.

The AI question, asked and answered — for now

Because the FAA has been deploying a new AI routing tool, reporters asked whether it was involved. Mullin said officials were "looking at that." The tool's maker, Air Space Intelligence, which holds the FAA's $875 million, 12-year SMART contract, denied any connection: the ground stop "is not based on or a result of the SMART system," the company said.

Officials also separated Friday's failure from the week's other big outage. Microsoft said it had no indication the FAA ground stop was related to its separate global service disruption, which began Thursday.

The bill now goes to Congress

The ground stop was the second nationwide halt of all departures since the September 11, 2001 attacks, after a brief one in January 2023. Duffy is asking Congress for up to $50 billion to replace the aging system — the administration's argument being that Friday's failure, which left airlines working through a backlog expected to take days to clear and more than 700 further cancellations already counted for Saturday, is what deferred modernisation costs in practice.

For travellers, the immediate position is this: departures resumed Friday evening, but Friday's 5,117 cancellations roll into the weekend schedule. Anyone flying in the US this weekend should check their flight's status with the airline before leaving for the airport, rather than relying on the original booking time.
